passage:
Lokesh's diary, Saturday
Our town's stepwell is just a dry, smelly pit now. I always thought it was boring. Today Anand Uncle, who runs the reading room near the bus stand, took four of us there and told us how it was built.
Long ago there was a drought for three years. The rich family wanted to dig a well only for their own fields. An old woman who sold curd said, "Water that belongs to one house dries up in one house." So the whole town dug together, even kids carried baskets of mud.
Anand Uncle said that's why the steps go down on all four sides: so nobody has to wait for anyone else.
I looked at the steps differently after that. I'm going to draw them tomorrow.

qa.q: Why do the stepwell's steps go down on all four sides, according to Anand Uncle?
qa.a: So nobody has to wait for anyone else.

qa.q: How did Lokesh's feelings about the stepwell change?
qa.a: Lokesh first found the stepwell boring, but after the story felt curious and interested enough to want to draw the steps.

qa.q: How could a teacher use a local story like this in class?
qa.a: A teacher could take students to the place, tell its story, and ask what the town's choice teaches about sharing today.

qa.q: How might Anand Uncle feel when the children look at the steps differently?
qa.a: Anand Uncle might feel pleased and hopeful that the town's history, and its lesson about sharing, will be remembered.

grounding: Shows a child learning a piece of local history and its moral about sharing from a community elder.

passage:
On the last night of the Dussehra Ramlila, Tejas sat on the school ground in his village, bored. He had seen Ravana burn every year.
"Why does Nani care so much?" he muttered.
Simran, his cousin, pulled him to where Nani sat on a mat. Nani pointed at the stage made of bullock carts. "Seventy years ago the river flooded the temple yard. Everyone said, no Ramlila this year. My father said the story is for hard years most of all. So they joined carts and did it here."
Tejas watched the actor playing Hanuman leap across the carts. "So that's why it's on carts?"
"That's why," said Simran. "We're sitting in the flood story too."
When the effigy caught fire, Tejas clapped louder than usual.

qa.q: What was the Ramlila stage made of?
qa.a: The stage was made of bullock carts.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling at the start of the evening, and what shows it?
qa.a: Tejas felt bored, because he sat muttering that he had seen Ravana burn every year.

qa.q: What small step helped Tejas care about the Ramlila?
qa.a: Simran taking him to Nani to hear the flood story connected the old epic to his own village's history.

qa.q: How does Nani see the Ramlila differently from Tejas at first?
qa.a: For Nani it holds her family's memory of getting through a hard year, not just a show she has seen before.

grounding: Illustrates a child connecting an epic performance to the local history and meaning his family attaches to it.

passage:
The lanterns were already swinging along the Hanoi street when Liam arrived for his first Mid-Autumn Festival. Tuan handed him a paper star lantern and pointed at the full moon.
"See the dark patch? That's Cuoi, sitting under a banyan tree."
"Why is he stuck up there?"
Tuan told it the way his grandmother did. Cuoi's magic banyan tree could heal people, but it had one rule: never water it with dirty water. Cuoi forgot, the tree flew up to the sky, and he grabbed its roots and went with it.
"So the moral is… keep promises?" Liam asked.
"Grandma says it's that small carelessness can cost big things."
Liam looked up again. The dark patch did look like someone sitting, waiting.

qa.q: What rule came with Cuoi's magic banyan tree?
qa.a: Never water it with dirty water.

qa.q: What does Liam's question about the moral suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: Liam seemed curious and interested, trying to understand the meaning of the story, not just the plot.

qa.q: How could Tuan make the story even more meaningful for Liam?
qa.a: Tuan could ask Liam if there is a moon story in his own family, so they can compare what each teaches.

qa.q: What is it like for Tuan to tell the story the way his grandmother does?
qa.a: Tuan probably feels proud and close to his grandmother, passing on her words to a new friend.

grounding: Shows a child sharing a festival folk tale and its moral with a visiting friend.

passage:
In the school lunch room, Sumit opened his tiffin: plain roti and moong, no onion, no garlic. Two boys at the table sniffed.
"Again boring food?"
"It's Paryushan," Sumit said. "We don't eat root vegetables for these days."
"Why? Potatoes don't have feelings," one boy laughed.
Sachin, who had been about to laugh too, stopped. He actually wanted to know. "Wait, why root vegetables?"
Sumit explained that pulling them up kills the whole plant and lots of tiny life in the soil, and his family tries to harm less during these days.
Sachin thought about it. "That's kind of big." Next day he left the potato sabzi out of his tiffin when he sat with Sumit, just to see how it felt.

qa.q: What was in Sumit's tiffin?
qa.a: Plain roti and moong, no onion, no garlic.

qa.q: Why did Sachin stop himself from laughing?
qa.a: Sachin felt curious and wanted to understand, and the joke suddenly seemed unkind next to Sumit's reason.

qa.q: How could a teacher help the lunch table understand Sumit's practice?
qa.a: A teacher could invite students to share their festival or food customs, so differences are explained and not mocked.

qa.q: What is it like for Sumit when his food is called boring every day?
qa.a: It may feel tiring and hurtful for Sumit, having to defend his faith over lunch instead of just eating.

grounding: Illustrates a child choosing to learn about and respect a classmate's religious practice instead of mocking it.

passage:
I'm Tanuja. I'll tell you what I saw on Christmas Eve in our colony.
Mrs D'Costa had set up a crib under the stairs, with clay figures and cotton for snow. Most of us just grabbed the plum cake and ran. Neelam didn't. She crouched and asked what each figure was, even the donkey. Mrs D'Costa explained the shepherds and the star. Neelam kept nodding.
When the carollers stopped for a prayer, some kids kept talking. Neelam put her finger to her lips and stood still with her hands folded, though her family goes to the temple, not church.
Afterwards Mrs D'Costa gave her an extra slice. I don't know exactly what Neelam was thinking. She looked like someone who'd been let into a secret.

qa.q: What did Mrs D'Costa use for snow in the crib?
qa.a: She used cotton for snow.

qa.q: What does Neelam's expression afterwards suggest, according to Tanuja?
qa.a: Neelam seemed delighted and moved, like someone who'd been let into a secret, though Tanuja can't be sure.

qa.q: What would you advise the kids who kept talking during the prayer?
qa.a: Even if it isn't your own faith, stay quiet for a few moments; it shows respect and costs nothing.

qa.q: How might Mrs D'Costa have felt about Neelam's questions?
qa.a: Mrs D'Costa probably felt touched and valued, since someone from another faith cared enough to ask about her festival.

grounding: Shows, through a neighbour's eyes, a child learning about and respecting a festival of another faith.

passage:
Monday, the week of Navroz. Ira said the fire temple was "weird" because she wasn't allowed inside. Zubin went quiet and didn't share his chips at break.
Wednesday. Ira asked him why he was sulking. Zubin said, "It's not weird. It's just ours." He explained that the fire has been kept burning for years and years, and only Parsis go in. Ira said, "That's not fair to me." Zubin shrugged: "Your family's puja room isn't for everyone either."
Ira thought about that all afternoon.
Saturday. Zubin's mother invited her for Navroz lunch. Ira sat outside the temple gate while they prayed, then ate sali boti and falooda at their table. "Thanks for waiting," Zubin said. She said, "It's your place. I get it now."

qa.q: What did Ira eat at Zubin's Navroz lunch?
qa.a: Ira ate sali boti and falooda.

qa.q: Why did Zubin go quiet and not share his chips on Monday?
qa.a: Zubin felt hurt and offended that Ira called his fire temple weird.

qa.q: Which comparison helped Ira understand, and why?
qa.a: Zubin compared the temple to her family's puja room, which let her see the rule from her own experience.

qa.q: How might Zubin's mother see Ira waiting at the gate?
qa.a: His mother might feel respected and warm towards Ira, seeing she honoured their custom instead of complaining.

grounding: Illustrates a child, over several days, moving from calling another faith's practice weird to respecting it.

passage:
Every morning before school, Kalyani goes with her grandmother to light the lamp at the tulsi in their courtyard. They stand quietly for a minute, then Kalyani says three things she's thankful for, out loud but softly. Today it was: the rain last night, Paati's knee not hurting, and the new pencil box.
Noor, from the next house, came to walk with her to school and waited by the gate. Kalyani's Paati waved her in. "Stand with us if you like, child."
Noor stood, a little shy. When they finished, Noor said, "At home, Nana says thanks before eating too. In his own words."
Kalyani grinned. "Tomorrow you tell one thing." Noor thought about it all the way to the bus stop.

qa.q: What were Kalyani's three thankful things today?
qa.a: The rain last night, Paati's knee not hurting, and the new pencil box.

qa.q: How was Noor probably feeling when Paati waved her in?
qa.a: Noor was probably a little shy and unsure, standing with a family during their prayer.

qa.q: How could Kalyani's family keep the habit welcoming for friends like Noor?
qa.a: They can keep it short and simple, like the thankful things, and let Noor share in her own words without having to copy their ritual.

qa.q: How might Paati feel seeing the two girls walk off together?
qa.a: Paati might feel happy and content that the small gratitude habit is shared between neighbours of different faiths.

grounding: Shows a child's daily ritual of silence and gratitude and a friend from another faith joining respectfully.

passage:
On Chuseok morning, Soo-ah's family set up the table for the ancestral rite in their Seoul apartment: rice cakes, pears, fish, a photo of Grandma in the middle. Her cousin Sami, visiting from Busan, kept poking the pears and whispering jokes.
When they bowed, Soo-ah kept her forehead on the floor longer than usual. She thought about Grandma teaching her to fold dumplings last Chuseok and her floury hands. She felt her throat get tight.
Afterwards Sami asked, "Why were you down there so long?"
"I was saying thank you," Soo-ah said. "For the dumplings."
Sami was quiet. At the next bow, he stayed still too, with his eyes shut, and didn't poke anything.

qa.q: Whose photo was in the middle of the table?
qa.a: A photo of Grandma was in the middle of the table.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah feeling while she bowed?
qa.a: Soo-ah felt grateful and a little sad, missing Grandma, which is why her throat got tight.

qa.q: How could an adult help a fidgety child like Sami take part in the rite?
qa.a: An adult could quietly explain what the bow means and suggest one person to think of, so it feels real rather than boring.

qa.q: How does Sami's view of the rite change after Soo-ah explains?
qa.a: Sami seems to see it as a real moment of remembering, not a ritual to joke through, so he joins in quietly.

grounding: Illustrates a child using a family ritual as a moment of silent gratitude and remembrance.

passage:
In January, the school started one minute of silence after lunch. Everyone put heads down; then you could write one line in a gratitude notebook. Sachin thought it was pointless. He doodled cricket bats instead.
Manoj, at the next desk, wrote something every day and never showed anyone.
Then came a bad Thursday. Sachin failed a maths test and got shouted at in PE. At the silence, he put his head down just to hide his face. The room was quiet. The heater ticked. After a while his shoulders stopped feeling like rocks.
When the bell went, he opened the notebook and wrote, slowly: "Manoj lent me his jumper at PE."
Manoj saw, and grinned, and didn't say anything.

qa.q: What did Sachin write in the notebook on Thursday?
qa.a: He wrote, "Manoj lent me his jumper at PE."

qa.q: Why did Sachin put his head down on the bad Thursday?
qa.a: Sachin felt upset and embarrassed after failing a maths test and being shouted at, so he wanted to hide his face.

qa.q: What small change could help students who find the silence pointless?
qa.a: The school could explain it isn't a test; you can just rest, and nobody checks what you write.

qa.q: If you were Manoj, what would you want after seeing Sachin's line?
qa.a: You'd probably feel pleased and touched, and want to keep it quiet so Sachin doesn't feel embarrassed.

grounding: Shows a child slowly finding value in a short school practice of silence and gratitude.

passage:
Summer activity club, week 4. Notes by Shankar, supervisor.
Afreen has tried everything we offer: chess (left after one game), dance (enthusiastic for two days), cricket (spent most of the time talking). I had started to wonder if nothing would hold her.
This week we put out clay. She sat at the pottery wheel on Tuesday and did not look up for an hour and a half. When the bell rang she said "already?" and asked to stay. Her pot collapsed three times; she laughed and started again each time. On Thursday she came early and asked the potter about glazes.
I have told her parents what I saw. My plan: give her a regular wheel slot, but keep other activities open. At nine she doesn't need to choose forever.

qa.q: How long did Afreen sit at the wheel on Tuesday without looking up?
qa.a: Afreen did not look up for an hour and a half.

qa.q: What does Afreen's laughing when her pot collapsed suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt absorbed and happy enough in the work that failure didn't discourage her.

qa.q: What would you advise Afreen's parents after reading this note?
qa.a: Encourage the clay without turning it into pressure, and let her keep trying other things too.

qa.q: How might Shankar see the week compared with the first three?
qa.a: Shankar probably feels relieved and pleased, having seen for the first time what really holds Afreen's attention.

grounding: Illustrates, through a supervisor's note, a child trying many activities and one clearly absorbing her.

passage:
Makar Sankranti, 14 Jan
Diary, it's me, Parveen. Irfan Bhai said making a kite is boring, just buy one. I tried anyway. I cut the paper wrong twice. The third one worked!!
I forgot to eat lunch. Ammi had to call three times. I didn't even hear the neighbours' "kaipoche" shouts for ages because I was measuring the sticks.
Then it flew. Only for a little while before it went sideways into the neem tree, but it FLEW. Irfan said, "Okay, maybe not so boring."
Last month I tried the keyboard and gave up in a week. Painting too. This felt different. My hands wanted to keep going.
Tomorrow I'm going to try one with a longer tail. 🪁

qa.q: How many times did Parveen cut the paper wrong?
qa.a: Parveen cut the paper wrong twice.

qa.q: What does forgetting lunch suggest about how Parveen felt while making the kite?
qa.a: It suggests Parveen felt completely absorbed and excited, so deep in the work that hunger and noise faded.

qa.q: How could Ammi support this new interest?
qa.a: Ammi could give Parveen space and simple materials to keep building, without insisting it becomes a big hobby.

qa.q: How does Irfan see kite-making by the end of the day?
qa.a: Irfan seems a little impressed, admitting it's "maybe not so boring" once the kite flew.

grounding: Shows a child noticing, in a diary, that one activity absorbs attention in a way earlier ones didn't.

passage:
During the Pongal holidays in their village, Usha tried to do everything at once. She beat the thavil drum with her uncle until her wrists ached. She stirred the pongal pot till Paati shooed her away. She even tried milking the cow, which kicked the bucket over.
On the third morning, she sat on the step while her grandmother Lakshmi drew the kolam, white dots in rows, lines looping round them. "Can I try?"
Lakshmi gave her the rice flour. Usha's first lines wobbled. She wiped them and tried again. The sun got hot. Her cousins called her to play. She didn't hear.
When she finally looked up, half the courtyard was covered.
"You were gone somewhere," Lakshmi said, smiling.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi drawing on the third morning?
qa.a: Lakshmi was drawing the kolam, white dots in rows with lines looping round them.

qa.q: What does Usha not hearing her cousins suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests Usha was deeply absorbed and content, lost in the drawing.

qa.q: How could Lakshmi help Usha grow this interest?
qa.a: Lakshmi could keep giving her rice flour and teach her new patterns now and then, letting her practise at her own pace.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel seeing Usha cover half the courtyard?
qa.a: Lakshmi probably feels proud and pleased that her granddaughter has found something she loves in a family tradition.

grounding: Illustrates a child trying many festival activities and noticing which one absorbs her attention.

passage:
In Nairobi the water came only on Tuesdays and Fridays that month, and Amara's family filled every jerrycan. Her friend Yuki, whose family had just moved from Osaka, came over after school and turned on the kitchen tap to wash one cup.
"Stop!" Amara laughed, grabbing it. "That's tomorrow's cooking water."
Yuki went pink. "Sorry. In our old flat it never stopped."
Amara showed her the system: a bowl in the sink for washing, then that water goes to the plants; the rinse water flushes the toilet. Yuki started counting how many cups they used.
The next week Yuki came with a drawing of her own family's kitchen, with a new bowl in the sink and an arrow to their balcony plants.

qa.q: On which days did the water come that month?
qa.a: The water came only on Tuesdays and Fridays.

qa.q: Why did Yuki go pink?
qa.a: Yuki felt embarrassed about wasting water without thinking, because it had never been scarce for her before.

qa.q: Which part of Amara's system could any family copy, and why?
qa.a: Reusing the washing bowl water for plants, because it's simple and saves water without extra cost.

qa.q: How might Amara feel when Yuki brings the drawing?
qa.a: Amara probably feels pleased and a little proud that her family's habits helped a friend change hers.

grounding: Shows children learning and spreading everyday water-saving habits.

passage:
It was May and the school felt like an oven, but when Zainab and Yamini walked past Class 6C at lunch, all four fans and the lights were on in an empty room.
"Every day," Zainab said. "Same in 6A."
They made a checklist on chart paper: fans off, lights off, taps closed. Each class would get a "last one out" monitor. Yamini drew a sweating sun on it so people would read it.
The first week, nobody bothered. The second week, Yamini went round at lunch and quietly switched things off herself. The third week, the headmistress read their chart aloud at assembly.
By June, 6C's monitor was the one reminding Zainab to switch off.

qa.q: What did Zainab and Yamini see in empty Class 6C at lunch?
qa.a: All four fans and the lights were on in an empty room.

qa.q: How do you think Yamini felt when nobody followed the checklist the first week?
qa.a: Yamini was likely disappointed and a bit frustrated, but determined, since she started switching things off herself.

qa.q: What went right in the third week that could help other schools?
qa.a: The headmistress backing the chart at assembly, because students take a habit more seriously when adults support it.

qa.q: How might the 6C monitor see the job by June?
qa.a: The monitor seems to feel responsible and proud, even reminding Zainab, the chart's own maker, to switch off.

grounding: Illustrates children starting an energy-saving habit in school during a hot season.

passage:
I'm Anand, from the flat across the landing. This Diwali I noticed Naveen doing strange things.
When gifts came, Naveen didn't tear the wrapping. Naveen folded it flat and put it in a box marked "next year". The sweets came in plastic trays; Naveen washed them and took them down to the aunty who sells flowers, for her marigolds.
On Diwali night the whole building was blazing. At midnight, Naveen went out and switched their string lights off, leaving just the clay diyas burning. I asked why.
"Lights on all night for nobody," Naveen said. "The diyas are prettier anyway."
I can't tell if Naveen is doing it for the planet or just likes order. But this year, our landing had a box for folded paper too. 🪔

qa.q: What did Naveen do with the plastic sweet trays?
qa.a: Naveen washed them and took them down to the aunty who sells flowers, for her marigolds.

qa.q: What does Naveen's answer about the lights suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Naveen was bothered by the waste but content with less, enjoying the diyas more than the blazing string lights.

qa.q: How could Naveen's family build on these habits?
qa.a: They could make the reuse box and the midnight switch-off a shared family routine, not just Naveen's.

qa.q: Why might Anand be unsure of Naveen's reasons?
qa.a: Anand is only watching from across the landing, so Anand can see the actions but not know what Naveen really thinks.

grounding: Shows, through a neighbour's eyes, a child reducing waste and saving energy during a festival.

passage:
In the Kinnaur village, Dolma's mother went to the apple orchard at dawn, so Dolma had to get her little sister Vinita ready for school. Vinita wouldn't put on her socks. Dolma was going to be late again.
"You always get the window seat on the bus. You always get Mola's stories first," Dolma snapped.
Their grandmother, Mola, was sitting by the stove. She said nothing, just handed Dolma a warm roti and pointed at Vinita's feet. "Cold socks. Warm them first."
Dolma held the socks near the stove. Vinita put them on at once.
That evening, Mola told the story to Dolma first. "Big sisters learn things first," she said. "Then they teach." Dolma sat a bit taller.

qa.q: Where did Dolma's mother go at dawn?
qa.a: She went to the apple orchard.

qa.q: Why did Dolma snap at Vinita?
qa.a: Dolma felt stressed about being late and jealous that Vinita always seemed to get the window seat and Mola's stories first.

qa.q: What small step helped with the socks, and what does it teach about caring for younger ones?
qa.a: Warming the socks first worked, because looking for the reason behind a little one's fuss often works better than pushing.

qa.q: How might Mola see the tension between her two granddaughters?
qa.a: Mola seems to understand both girls and, rather than scolding, quietly gives Dolma a way to feel valued as the elder.

grounding: Illustrates a child managing sibling jealousy, caring for a younger sister and learning from a grandparent.

passage:
For weeks before Lucia day in Uppsala, Vera had wanted to be Lucia at school. The teacher chose her little sister's class instead, and Ingrid got the crown of candles.
Vera slammed her bedroom door. "She's seven! She'll drop it."
Mormor came in with flour on her hands. "Come and help with the saffron buns. I need someone who can shape an S properly."
They twisted dough together. Mormor told her she had never been Lucia either. "I was the one who held the matches. Still remember it."
On the morning, Ingrid's crown slipped as she walked. Vera, in the front row, saw Ingrid's panicked face, stepped out and fixed a pin, fast. Ingrid walked on, glowing.
Afterwards Ingrid gave Vera the best bun.

qa.q: What did Mormor ask Vera to help make?
qa.a: Mormor asked her to help with the saffron buns.

qa.q: Why did Vera slam her bedroom door?
qa.a: Vera felt jealous and disappointed that Ingrid got the crown she had wanted for weeks.

qa.q: How did Mormor help Vera without scolding her?
qa.a: She gave Vera a job that needed her skill and shared that she had never been Lucia either, which eased the sting.

qa.q: What was it like for Ingrid when Vera fixed her crown?
qa.a: Ingrid was probably scared the crown would fall and then relieved and grateful that her big sister helped.

grounding: Shows a child moving from sibling rivalry to caring for a younger sister, helped by a grandparent's story.

passage:
Grandparents' Day at school fell in the last week of December, with a heater in the hall and tea in paper cups. Salma had practised a speech about her Dadi. Her little brother, from Class 2, kept grabbing the microphone and saying "My Dadi!" before her.
"He's ruining it," Salma hissed to her friend Gargi.
Dadi pulled Salma close. "When your Abbu was small, he did the same to his sister. She let him say one line, and then she said the rest. Everyone remembers her speech."
So Salma knelt, let her brother say "My Dadi makes the best sheer khurma," and then stood up and gave hers. The hall laughed at his line and clapped at hers. Gargi gave her a thumbs up.

qa.q: What line did Salma's little brother say into the microphone?
qa.a: He said, "My Dadi makes the best sheer khurma."

qa.q: What was Salma feeling when she hissed to Gargi?
qa.a: Salma felt frustrated and annoyed that her brother kept grabbing the microphone and, she thought, ruining her speech.

qa.q: Which idea from Dadi worked, and why?
qa.a: Letting her brother say one line first worked, because he got his turn and stopped competing, and Salma still gave her speech.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel watching both grandchildren speak about her?
qa.a: Dadi probably feels proud and loved, and pleased that her story helped Salma choose patience over a fight.

grounding: Illustrates a child handling sibling rivalry by learning from a grandparent's advice at a school event.

passage:
Three weeks before the board exams, the hostel study hall at night sounded like a railway station: whispers, phones buzzing, someone's snack packet. Anjali had made a revision chart: one subject per evening block, the hardest topics first, when she was freshest.
Karthik sat next to her and kept showing her videos. "Just one, it's funny."
She laughed once, then lost twenty minutes. The next night she moved to the corner desk by the wall and left her phone in her locker, telling Karthik, "Ask me at ten, not before."
In the chemistry mock, she hit a question she couldn't do. Her heart started racing. She remembered her plan: circle it, move on, come back. She finished the rest, returned, and got half of it.
Karthik copied her chart the next week.

qa.q: Where did Anjali leave her phone the next night?
qa.a: She left her phone in her locker and moved to the corner desk by the wall.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when she hit the question she couldn't do?
qa.a: Anjali felt a rush of panic, with her heart racing, but her plan helped her stay steady.

qa.q: What could Karthik take from Anjali's approach?
qa.a: Karthik could plan hard topics for fresh hours, keep the phone away during study blocks, and skip and return to stuck questions in exams.

qa.q: How might Karthik see Anjali moving to another desk?
qa.a: Karthik might feel a bit rejected at first, but later seems to see it as smart, since Karthik copies her chart.

grounding: Shows a teenager planning revision, resisting distraction and using a strategy to handle exam-room panic.

passage:
Hi Charu Didi,
You said to write down my plan, so here it is. Boards start on 2 March.
Mornings (6–8): maths, because my brain is best then. Evenings: one science, one language. Sundays: full past papers, timed, at the dining table, no music.
The big problem is the phone. Last week I "checked one thing" and it was 11 pm. So Papa is keeping it in his room from 7 to 10. I hated the idea, honestly. But the first night I finished two chapters.
What I don't know is how to stop panicking in the exam hall. You said you used to write "breathe" on your rough sheet. Did that really work, or were you just being nice?
Also, did you ever feel like everyone else was ahead?
Pankaj

qa.q: What does Pankaj plan to do on Sundays?
qa.a: Full past papers, timed, at the dining table, with no music.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel about handing the phone to Papa?
qa.a: Pankaj hated the idea at first and felt resentful, but was pleasantly surprised when he finished two chapters the first night.

qa.q: How could Charu Didi best answer Pankaj's question about exam-hall panic?
qa.a: She could share honestly what helped her, like a pause and slow breaths, and remind Pankaj that nerves are common, not a sign of failing.

qa.q: What is it like for Charu to get this email from her younger cousin?
qa.a: Charu may feel trusted and a little responsible, since Pankaj values her advice enough to plan around it.

grounding: Illustrates a teen planning revision, handling phone distraction and asking for help with exam nerves.

passage:
So you want to know how I survived the entrance exam? Honestly, Sharmila, it wasn't the studying. It was the ten minutes before.
I'm Gurleen, I'd done all the mocks. But in the waiting hall, a boy next to me was saying, "Did you do the rotation chapter? It's definitely coming." I hadn't revised it properly. My stomach just dropped.
I went to the washroom and splashed water on my face. And I told myself: you've done this paper forty times at home. Same format. Same clock. The strategy is the same: easy ones first, mark the hard ones, don't sit on one question more than a few minutes.
And yes, the rotation question came. I skipped it, finished the others, came back with fifteen minutes left. Got half marks. I cleared the cut-off anyway. So stay away from people revising loudly in the waiting hall, that's my whole advice.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do in the washroom?
qa.a: Gurleen splashed water on the face and remembered having done the paper forty times at home.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen's stomach drop in the waiting hall?

Debate club notes, week 6 (Payal, coach)
Zubin arrives with strong opinions and three facts. Today's motion was "Cities should ban private cars from the centre." Zubin opened well: less pollution, safer streets. When Aisha asked about shopkeepers losing customers, he said, "They'll adjust," and moved on. The room noticed.

Urmila had until 6 pm to confirm the class picnic bus, and the forecast said "30% chance of rain" for Sunday. The group chat had exploded.
Usha, her best friend, texted: "30% is basically zero, just book it!!" Someone else wrote: "30% means it'll rain for 30% of the day."

After the colony cricket match in Gangtok, Pema was showing off. "My batting average is 48. Yours is only 31, Dolma."
Dolma was drinking water on the steps. "How many innings?"
"Two."
"I've played twelve."
"So? Average is average."
Dolma picked up a stick and drew in the dust. "You got 90 once and 6 once. That's 48. I've got twelve scores, some high, some bad. If you'd got out for 2 today, you'd be at 32."
Pema stared at the dust. "That's… annoying."
"It's not bad. You're good. It's just two games don't tell much."
Pema kicked a stone. Then he grinned. "Okay, check me after twelve."

qa.q: How many innings had Pema played?
qa.a: Pema had played two innings.

qa.q: What does Pema's "That's… annoying" suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: Pema felt deflated and a little embarrassed, realising his impressive average rested on very few games.

qa.q: How did Dolma make her point without putting Pema down?
qa.a: Dolma showed the maths in the dust and also said "You're good," so the lesson was about numbers, not about him.

qa.q: If you were Dolma, what would you want Pema to understand?
qa.a: You'd want him to see that a few results can swing an average a lot, so bigger records are fairer to compare.

grounding: Shows a teen explaining why an average from very few cases can mislead.

Science teacher's note, Class 9, 12 August (Bhavna)
Ujjwal announced today that his "lucky blue socks" make him score higher, because he wore them for his three best tests. Half the class agreed they'd seen it.
Instead of arguing, I asked the class to check. What else happened on those three days? Ujjwal thought. All three were Mondays, after quiet Sundays at home. He also admitted he'd revised more for those tests because they were chapters he liked.
We drew a chart: socks, sleep, revision, topic, marks. The pattern with revision was clearer than with socks.
Ujjwal laughed, a bit embarrassed. "But I'm still wearing them." Fine by me. The point is he now asks what else changed. Next week: I'll ask each student to test one "lucky" belief.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal claim about his blue socks?
qa.a: He said his lucky blue socks make him score higher, because he wore them for his three best tests.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel when the chart showed revision mattered more?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt a bit embarrassed but amused, laughing and deciding to keep the socks anyway.

qa.q: Which part of Bhavna's approach worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking the class to check what else happened on those days worked, because it let students discover other causes instead of just being told.

qa.q: How might the classmates who agreed with Ujjwal see the chart?
qa.a: They might feel surprised, and realise that seeing something happen together doesn't mean one thing caused the other.

grounding: Illustrates a teacher helping a teen tell a coincidence apart from a cause by looking for other factors.

Diary, Vijay here. The news said kids who eat breakfast get better marks. Jaya, my sister, immediately said, "See? Breakfast makes you smart. Eat your poha."
